As a developer, it’s easy to fall into a false sense of security: "I wrote the React form, I used HTML5 validation, and I even have a regex check in my state handler. My backend is safe." entry.title: ¡El z80, el procesador más poderoso!
entry.summary:
¡Notición! En 1982, se hizo popularísimo un ordenador, el Sinclair ZX Spectrum. El corazón de este ordenador era un z80, un microprocesador también muy popular por su fiabilidad y relación precio/rendimiento. En aquella época, el telón de acero estaba en plena vigencia, y los países del bloque del este mantuvieron durante muchísimos años estos ordenadores, mejorándolos y parcheándolos para que fueran capaces de mantener el tipo frente a la carga cada vez mayor de trabajo. El aislamiento de estos países llevó a la exploración profunda y optimización de estos micros. Pero... ¿cómo pudieron hacerlo? Al fin y al cabo, las tareas a realizar en el día a día resultan realmente demandantes: procesamiento de textos, correo electrónico, y claro... la web. Resulta que ahora se ha hecho público el secreto que encontraron los informáticos rusos: el z80 es mucho más capaz de lo que nos habían contado. La caché de la línea de ejecución estaba presente en los z80, pero... ¡deshabilitada! Los Sinclair ZX Spectrum llevaban este micro. Un programa como el siguiente, que pokea una pequeña rutina habilita la caché, liberando toda la capacidad del micro. 10 REM ** Power unblocker ** 20 CLS 30 RESTORE 40 READ x: IF x=0 THEN GO TO 100 50 LET x=x+30: POKE 40000,x 60 PRINT CHR$ (x); 70 GO TO 40 1000 DATA 43,80,81,69,71,80,86,71,2,20,18,20,23,3,0
Pero, exactamente, ¿cuánto? Bien, si migramos el algoritmo del famoso programa de benchmarking CPUz, y lo ejecutamos, lo que resulta es sorprendente...
¡Un i9 de última generación "solo" obtiene una puntuación de 952, mientras que el z80 liberado se va hasta los 1100! Por supuesto, esto no incluye los cálculos en concurrencia con múltiples cores, ya que el z80 solo tiene uno. En cualquier caso, una gran noticia que seguramente hará que el fabricante se anime a vender micros z80 desbloqueados, un año después de haber detenido su producción. En la parte negativa, seguramente esto provocará que todo lo retro que use un z80 como corazón vea su precio encarecido de forma aberrante.

entry.title: That Dreaded Alembic NotNullViolation Error (and How to Survive It)
entry.summary:
What Happened?
Imagine you have a table called organizations full of precious data. You decide: Hey, let’s add a new column called plan! Sounds harmless, right? Wrong. You add it as NOT NULL, meaning every row must have a value. But wait… your table is already filled with rows. PostgreSQL looks at them and says: This isn’t a bug in Alembic or SQLAlchemy. It’s PostgreSQL protecting your precious data. Adding a NOT NULL column to existing data without a default is basically like asking someone to fill out a survey you didn’t give them in advance. They don’t know what to answer, so they freak out. You’ve got a few ways to make PostgreSQL happy again: op.add_column( 'organizations', sa.Column('plan', sa.String(), nullable=False, server_default='free') )
Existing rows get a value ('free') automatically. After the migration, you can remove the default if you like. Quick, painless, and everyone’s happy. Add the column as nullable: op.add_column( 'organizations', sa.Column('plan', sa.String(), nullable=True) )
Update existing rows: UPDATE organizations SET plan = 'free' WHERE plan IS NULL;
op.alter_column('organizations', 'plan', nullable=False) More steps, but more control. Good if you need custom logic per row. Before Alembic touches anything, manually update the table: Then run your migration. Old rows are ready, and PostgreSQL doesn’t throw a tantrum. Adding a NOT NULL column to a table with existing rows is like adding a new rule to a crowded party: someone will get upset if you don’t provide a plan. Always think about existing data. Give PostgreSQL a default, update the old rows, or do both. And remember: Alembic errors might look scary, but they’re really just your database’s way of saying: “Hey, I love your data too much to let it break. Let’s do this right.”

entry.title: Avoiding Dashboard Dead Ends: Why Tableau Calculated Fields Must Be Clearly Defined
entry.summary: At some point in most analytics roles, you realise that the biggest risk to a dashboard isn’t poor visual design—it’s unclear data. Calculated fields that aren’t documented, tables with ambiguous names, and metrics that mean different things to different people can quietly undermine trust and slow delivery. **When Flexibility Becomes a Risk Core, trusted business tables Temporary or experimental tables Calculated fields with hidden filters or assumptions Over time, this can lead to dozens—or even thousands—of similarly named tables, each with unclear provenance. What initially feels empowering can quickly turn into a maintenance challenge. **The Problem With “Obvious” Metrics **When Documentation Isn’t Designed for the End User **The Trust Problem: “Can We Use This?” **Where Should Documentation Live? Internal company pages or wikis are accessible, but can quickly become outdated. Google Docs are easy to collaborate on, but lack strong governance. Within Tableau dashboards (descriptions, tooltips, captions) keeps context close to the data. Metadata layers or data catalogues can help, though adoption varies across organisations. Often, a hybrid approach works best—keeping high-level definitions close to dashboards while maintaining deeper technical documentation elsewhere. **The Reality of Data Dictionaries **Safeguarding, Not Bureaucracy **The Bottom Line **Undocumented calculated fields don’t just create confusion—they create delays, rework, and mistrust. Over time, they can turn dashboards into dead ends rather than decision-support tools. Clear definitions, accessible documentation, and thoughtful governance are not administrative overheads. They are foundations of reliable analytics. Dashboards should move organisations forward, not leave analysts and stakeholders second-guessing the data behind them.
